```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(modelsummary)
library(knitr)

# --- Replace this block with loading YOUR data ---------------

data <- mtcars

# Example analysis: does a car's weight predict its fuel economy?
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = data)

# Pull values out so they can be reported inline (never hard-type a number)
r2      <- summary(model)$r.squared
wt_beta <- coef(model)[["wt"]]
n_obs   <- nrow(data)
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Election polls have a vital role in examining voter preferences and influencing expectations about electoral results. However, their stated precision does not automatically guarantee accuracy. In the Journal of the American Statistical Association, @shiranimehr2018 discovered that observed polling errors were around double the implied conventional margins of error, emphasising that polling uncertainty extends beyond random sampling variability. This prompts a question about whether polling characteristics can explain differences in the accuracy of polls.

The 2012 and 2016 US presidential elections offer a valuable basis for exploring this question. Particularly, state-level polling in the election year 2016 demonstrated substantial errors, with @kennedy2018 noting a mean absolute error of 5.1 percentage points. The journal article states that late swings in voter preferences and insufficient adjustments for educational attainment were key factors that led to such errors.

These findings further motivate an examination into whether polling timing, sample size, and survey methodology are associated with the accuracy of polling results. Hence, this report investigates the research question: **To what degree are polling timing, sample size and methodology associated with the accuracy of state-level presidential polls for the 2012 and 2016 elections.** More specifically, it explores:

1\. Whether polling accuracy is associated with days prior to Election Day

2\. Whether election year, sample size and methodology explain variation in polling errors once timing is accounted for

3\. Whether relationship between polling timing and error is different across the two election years

Polling accuracy is measured as the absolute error between polling and actual Democratic-Republican voting margins. Multiple linear regression models are utilised as a means to explore these relationships.

## Data

Describe the data accurately: its source, the unit of observation, the variables used, and any cleaning or exclusions. The example uses the built-in `mtcars` data [@rcore], covering `r n_obs` vehicles. Summarise the key variables as in @tbl-descriptives.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptives
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of the variables used in the analysis."
data |>
  summarise(
    across(c(mpg, wt, hp),
           list(mean = mean, sd = sd),
           .names = "{.col}_{.fn}")

  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c("Variable", ".value"),
               names_sep = "_") |>
```

# Results {#sec-results}

<!-- See rubric: Results - describe analysis w.r.t. the question; visualise; check assumptions. -->

@fig-relationship shows the relationship between weight and fuel economy, with a fitted regression line. The estimated model is reported in @tbl-model: each additional 1000 lbs is associated with a change of `r round(wt_beta, 1)` mpg, and the model explains `r round(100 * r2, 1)`% of the variation in fuel economy. Model assumptions are checked in @sec-appendix.

```{r}
#| label: fig-relationship
#| fig-cap: "Fuel economy against vehicle weight, with a fitted linear regression line and 95% confidence band."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(data, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Fuel economy (mpg)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of fuel economy (mpg) on weight and horsepower."
# modelsummary's default `tinytable` backend renders cleanly to PDF.
modelsummary(
  list("Fuel economy (mpg)" = model),
  coef_map = c("wt" = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
               "hp" = "Horsepower",
               "(Intercept)" = "Intercept"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared"),
  stars = TRUE
)
```

# Statistical appendix {#sec-appendix}

<!-- See rubric: Statistical appendix - fully reproducible, annotated analysis. -->

This appendix documents the analysis so the results above are fully reproducible. The annotated code reproduces the model and its assumption checks; the complete project (data, scripts, and commit history) is in the repository linked at the top.

## Model {#sec-app-model}

@tbl-model-detail reports the full fitted model with 95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-detail
#| tbl-cap: "Full regression results, with 95% confidence intervals."
#| echo: true
# Fit the model and report it as a formatted table (not raw console output)
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)

modelsummary(
  list("Fuel economy (mpg)" = model),
  statistic = "conf.int",                       # 95% CIs beneath each estimate
  coef_map  = c("wt" = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
                "hp" = "Horsepower",
                "(Intercept)" = "Intercept"),
  gof_map   = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared")
)
```

## Assumption checks {#sec-app-checks}

@fig-diagnostics shows the residual diagnostics used to check the linear-model assumptions of constant variance and approximately normal residuals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics: residuals vs fitted values (left) and a normal Q-Q plot (right)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(model, which = 1)   # residuals vs fitted: linearity and equal variance
plot(model, which = 2)   # normal Q-Q: normality of residuals
```
